content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
The paper proposes a domain adaptation problem with the source domain not available in addition to previous universal domain adaptation. The paper employs a two-stage training procedure to solve the problem.

In the first procurement stage, the paper aims to extend the source classification boundary to out-of-domain data and improve the ability of the source classifier to reject out-of-distribution samples. The proposed method generates negative data lying between clusters and far from the cluster centers and uses them to train the feature extractor, the classifier, and the backbone network. The idea of exploiting generated data has been used by previous works [1], but the paper proposes a novel generation method, which is new and useful for universal domain adaptation.

However, the generation process has some problems. First, the paper only considers the samples between two clusters. What if considering the samples between several clusters? For data in D_{n}^{(b)}, when the probability of the data is similar among three or more classes, labeling it as the largest two probability classes is sub-optimal. 

Secondly, when the target domain is far from the source domain, target data belonging to the shared classes will be in the area of D_{n}^{(b)}. The classifier will classify these target data as the classes in C_n, which will assign high w'(x_t) in the second deployment stage and degrade the performance.

Thirdly, there is no theoretical guarantee of how many samples are enough or how to sample a complete set to cover all out-of-distribution areas.

In the second deployment stage, the paper uses the sum of the exponential probability of shared and private classes. As stated above, with the first stage, the target shared data are not necessary to have a low probability in the private classes. The performance can be degraded.

The loss for the second stage is more like a pseudo-labeling method to use the binary pseudo-label of 'shared' or 'private' obtained from the model in the first stage. The paper needs to provide an error bound on the final classification result with respect to the error in pseudo-labeling.

The paper fails to report the influence of the number of samples on the final performance, which is essential to the generative model based methods.



Minor points: 
The notation is a little messy, such as what is the relation between D_{n} and D_{n}^{(a)}, D_{n}^{(b)}.

[1] Hoffman, Judy, et al. "Cycada: Cycle-consistent adversarial domain adaptation." arXiv preprint arXiv:1711.03213 (2017).

content.title: Reply (2/2) to Official Blind Review #3
content.comment:
... Reply continued from the first thread.

4. “guarantee”

- To demonstrate the stability of our method for a successful adaptation, we have performed extensive experiments and sensitivity analysis across varied 
a) datasets (Sec. 4.3a, Tab. 1, Tab. 2, Fig. 8)
b) category-gap (Sec. 4.3d, Fig. 6, Fig. 7, Sec. 4.3e, Sec. C.5, Tab. 4, Fig. 8A)
c) procurement hyperparameters (Sec. 4.3c, Sec. Fig. 5C, Sec. C.4, Fig. 8B), 
d) deployment hyperparameters (Fig. 5B), 
e) number of samples and negative classes (Sec. 4.3f, Fig 8, Fig. 5C). 
f) varied backbone initialization (Sec. C.1)
Moreover the sensitivity curves in (Fig. 8A) demonstrate the influence of the chosen hyperparameters in the performance across varied adaptation settings.

- Furthermore, in Sec. 4.3e, we have also extended our method to the recognition of new classes using one-shot incremental samples. Here, our method significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art [1] (almost five times better). This is attributed to a high degree of intra-class compactness with inter-class separability as shown in Fig. 9 (Sec. C.8), corroborating a superior adaptation guarantee.


5. “Notation”: 

We acknowledge a slight abuse of notation. To clarify, D_{n} was meant to be a generic representation of a negative dataset. D_{n}^{(a)} would follow the definition of D_{n} (page 2, last para), since it is defined in the image space. D_{n}^{(b)} required a separate notation, which has been defined in Sec. 3.1. We shall make it more evident in a later revision.


References
=========
[1] You et al. “Universal domain adaptation” CVPR 2019
[2] Cao et al. "Partial transfer learning with selective adversarial networks" CVPR 2018
[3] Liu et al. "Separate to Adapt: Open Set Domain Adaptation via Progressive Separation" CVPR 2019
[4] Zhang et al. “Importance weighted adversarial nets for partial domain adaptation” CVPR 2018

content.title: Reply (1/2) to Official Blind Review #3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback. We hope the following will help address the reviewer’s concerns.


1. “Considering the samples between several clusters”, “out-of-distribution areas”

- We have already discussed the use of more than 2 classes in Sec 4.3f. For instance, one can composite 3 images and produce nC3 negative classes. In a similar fashion, one can create an arbitrary number of negative classes using the source clusters for D_n^{(b)}. 

- Essentially, we do not impose constraints about which source classes are chosen, or how many negative classes are created. We show an ablation with an arbitrary number of negative classes in Fig. 5C and Fig. 8A. However, to avoid a huge array of experiments, we fixed the number of negative classes to nC2 for our experiments (unless otherwise stated).

- Additionally, the negligible computation cost of the negative sample generation algorithms (for both D_n^{(a)} and D_n^{(b)}), allows one to generate a large amount of negative samples, even during training. As the sampling is done randomly (Sec. B.1b), i.e. a different set of samples are generated at each iteration (similar to online augmentation), one can always expect to cover a large portion of out-of-distribution areas, over multiple training iterations. Nevertheless, we have already provided the number of negative samples we chose for each dataset in Sec. B.1b.


2. “Target domain is far from the source domain”

- Please see the results in Table 2 (VisDA dataset) where we outperform all other methods in the presence of a large domain-gap (computer generated 3D models, and real-world images), and especially, the previous state-of-the-art UAN [1] in both metrics, T_{avg} and T_{unk}.

- In the Universal Domain Adaptation problem, in a completely unsupervised setting with no knowledge of the degree of domain-gap or the category-gap, there is no way to determine the extent to which the domain-gap or the category-gap will affect the performance. It is indeed an open problem in the machine learning community. Therefore, the only way to corroborate the effectiveness of one approach over the other is to empirically demonstrate the performance across a large spectrum of domain-gap and category-gap.

- Several recent approaches [1, 2, 3, 4] train a domain discriminator by leveraging data from both domains, to minimize an instance-weighted adaptation loss, and hope for the right samples to be given a higher weight. Even these do not guarantee success in the presence of a large domain shift. 

- In the source-free setting, our approach to learn out-of-distribution detection could be viewed as a way to learn a *source* vs *not-source* discriminator, in contrast to *source* vs *target* discriminator in the prior works [1, 2, 3, 4]. Thus, the SSM weight is at least as reliable as the existing approaches, with the additional flexibility of being applied to any target domain (other methods require a unique discriminator for each source-target pair). We have empirically verified the effectiveness of SSM in Sec. 4.3b.


3. “influence of the number of samples on the final performance”

- We have reported the influence of number samples on the final performance. Specifically, in Fig. 8B, we have reported the adaptation performance on varied batch ratios.

- In the absence of any knowledge of the category gap, forecasting the influence of the number of samples on adaptation is out of the question. Empirically, we found that a balanced batch always resulted in an optimal performance (see Fig. 8B).


Reply continued to the next thread…


References
=========
[1] You et al. “Universal domain adaptation” CVPR 2019
[2] Cao et al. "Partial transfer learning with selective adversarial networks" CVPR 2018
[3] Liu et al. "Separate to Adapt: Open Set Domain Adaptation via Progressive Separation" CVPR 2019
[4] Zhang et al. “Importance weighted adversarial nets for partial domain adaptation” CVPR 2018

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
In this paper, the authors studied a so-called source-free domain adaptation problem. They aimed to propose a universal DA method for different relationships between the target label set and the source label set, without accessing the source domain data in the adaptation phase.

The problem studied is an interesting and practical problem for domain adaptation. The proposed solution looks promising at the high level. However, there are some major concerns.

1. The term "source-free" is misleading. Indeed, a "source domain" is needed in the procurement stage. Based on the the proposed method, there is still an assumption on the source domain, i.e., there is an overlapping label set between the source domain and the target domain. Given a target domain, if there are not overlapping labels between the target domain and the source domain, the proposed method will fail to work. In this sense, the term "universal" is also misleading.

2. In the proposed procurement stage, a key step is to generate the so-called "negative" source instances. The authors proposed two heuristic approaches, one for image data, and the other for non-image data. These two approaches looks okay, but not convincing as no deeper analysis is provided. Moreover, in experiments, only the image domain is used. The effectiveness of the approach for non-image negative instances generation is not verified.

3. In prediction, for the case where the target domain has a set of private labels, the proposed method can only predict all instances of private labels as "unknown" if successful. This may not be useful in practice. 

Here are the minor concerns:
1. Authors attempted to compress much content into 9 pages, which makes to the paper a little difficult to follow.

2. In the literature of transfer learning or domain adaptation, a similar problem setup was studied around 10 years ago, which was focused on the application of web text mining. 
"Xiang et al., Source-Selection-Free Transfer Learning, IJCAI-11"

content.title: Reply to Official Blind Review #2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback. We hope the following will help address the reviewer’s concerns.

1. “Source-free”:

- As the title suggests, source-free implies **source-free adaptation**, i.e. the case where “source and target samples never coexist together during training” (Sec. 3.1.1, para 2). 

- A source domain is only used to acquire the knowledge of “class-separability criterion” in the source model. One can not expect a randomly initialized neural network to learn classification using unlabeled images. Thus, unsupervised domain adaptation is entirely different from other unsupervised learning tasks (e.g., clustering), where a model doesn’t require any task-specific knowledge (such as the class-separability knowledge required in classification). 

- In our case, the best analogy could be, data-free knowledge distillation [2, 3], where a teacher model is trained on a dataset and then transfers the knowledge to a student model without using the source data.


2. “Universal”: 

- We already report the case when there are **no overlapping labels** between the source and the target domains (please see Sec. 4.3e). Thus, our method does not necessarily require shared classes. In this way, our method is truly universal.

- On a side note, we do not claim to propose the “universal” setting - it is a published work [1], and the previous state-of-the-art. However, we demonstrate the superior performance and stability of our method over [1], on a wide range of datasets and category-gaps (Sec. 4.3d, Fig. 6, Sec. C.5, Fig. 7, Sec. C.4, Fig. 8). This corroborates the applicability of our method in the universal setting.


3. “Unknown”: 

- In Sec. 4.3e, we extend our method to the recognition of new classes using one-shot incremental samples, where USFDA’s performance is almost five times that of [1]. Thus, the proposed method has a practical applicability, beyond the “unknown” classification.

- The assignment of “unknown” label to target-private classes is a standard protocol in DA (see VisDA2018 Open-Set Classification challenge [4]). The same is followed in the Universal DA setting proposed by [1].

- In a completely unsupervised scenario (no labeled target instance), one can not assign a semantic label to unseen classes with high precision. However, the success of our method in Sec. 4.3e is attributed to a high degree of intra-class compactness and inter-class separability which is clearly validated by visualizing the feature space in Fig. 9 (Sec. C.8). Therefore, USFDA is much more useful in practice.


4. “Non-image negative instances”:

- To the best of our knowledge, the universal setting has been introduced by [1], as is claimed by the authors. Owing to the time and space constraints, and the availability of extensive datasets, for a fair evaluation we limited the number of experiments to the visual domain adaptation scenario, where the universal setting is proposed. Nevertheless, our method is easily applicable across domains, should a future work require so. We would appreciate if the reviewer cites some publicly available datasets other than image datasets, for the Universal Domain Adaptation setting.


5. Regarding “Source-Selection-Free Transfer Learning” (SSFTL):

- We would like to emphasize on the key differences:
a) SSFTL considers access to a large scale information source, and states that the “source data for transfer learning can be hidden somewhere within this large online information source”. Hence it is much similar to the partial domain adaptation scenario (Y_t ⊂ Y_{tag})
b) Furthermore, SSFTL assumes access to labeled target instances (Sec. 2.1 of [5]). Hence it is not fully unsupervised.
c) Moreover, the assumption of access to a large scale dataset clearly violates the source-free assumption. Thus, this work is stated as “source-selection-free” and not “source-free”.


References
=========
[1] You et al. “Universal domain adaptation” CVPR 2019
[2] Nayak et al. “Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks” ICML 2019
[3] Lopes et al. "Data-free knowledge distillation for deep neural networks" arXiv preprint arXiv:1710.07535 (2017)
[4] https://ai.bu.edu/visda-2018/
[5] Xiang et al. "Source-Selection-Free Transfer Learning" IJCAI-11

content.review:
This interesting paper on an important topic is extremely hard to read because it assumes that the reader is deeply familiar with the Domain Adaptation. In order to make the paper more accessible to a general audience, the authors should:
1) follow the 1st sentence in the abstract by a new sentence that provides an intuitive example the idea of domain shift from labeled source to unlabeled target domain  
2)  re-organize the current intro, which reads more like related work, into a more traditional format
     - one intuitive paragraph about domain adaptation, source/target domain, and domain shift; provide at least one compelling  illustrative example from a real-world application
     - one intuitive paragraph with an illustrative example on how the proposed approach will help solve a problem; at the same intuitive level, compare-and-contrast it with existing approaches
     - one intuitive, in-detail paragraph on how the proposed approach works
     - one paragraph summarizing the main findings/results 
3) ideally, add a section with an illustrative running example, which would have a huge impact on the paper's readability

content.title: Reply to Official Blind Review #1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the comments on readability.

Our major contribution in this work is the universal source-free setting. Thus, given the space constraints, we focused more on describing the setting, assuming a basic knowledge of Domain Adaptation. We shall make the introduction more lucid in a later revision.

Further, we would appreciate a constructive discussion on the primary contributions of our work.
